title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of acute bacterial meningitis in adults at a tertiary university hospital in Thailand (Medicine (Baltimore), 2024)

claims.text: In community-acquired bacterial meningitis (CBM), the most common organisms were Streptococcus agalactiae (29.0%), S. pneumoniae (12.2%), and S. suis (11.5%).
claims.byte_quote: Streptococcus agalactiae (29.0%; 100% penicillin-susceptible strains), S. pneumoniae (12.2%; 11.1% penicillin-intermediate strains and no penicillin-resistant strain), and S. suis (11.5%; 6.7% penicillin-intermediate strains and no penicillin-resistant strain) were the most common organisms in CBM.

claims.text: In nosocomial bacterial meningitis (NBM), the most frequent organisms were Acinetobacter baumannii (18.7%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (16.0%), and Staphylococcus aureus (10.7%).
claims.byte_quote: The most frequently found organisms in NBM were A. baumannii (18.7%; 100% carbapenem-resistant strains and 100% colistin-susceptible strains), K. pneumoniae (16.0%; 50% ceftriaxone-resistant strains and 100% carbapenem-susceptible strains), and S. aureus (10.7%; 25% methicillin-resistant strains and 100% vancomycin-susceptible strains).

claims.text: Gram-positive cocci were more prevalent in CBM than NBM (78.6% vs 37.3%), whereas gram-negative bacilli were more common in NBM than CBM (57.3% vs 19.1%).
claims.byte_quote: Gram-positive cocci were more prevalent in CBM than in NBM (78.6% vs 37.3%, P < .001), whereas gram-negative bacilli were more common in NBM than in CBM (57.3% vs 19.1%, P < .001).

claims.text: A positive CSF Gram stain was found nonsignificantly more often in CBM than NBM (24.5% vs 11.8%).
claims.byte_quote: Positive Gram stain in CSF was nonsignificantly more frequently found in CBM than in NBM (24.5% vs 11.8%, P = .08).
